In brief

When the Citizen expresses contempt for King Edward, Joe, Alf, and J. J. are quick to join in. Hynes recalls "the priests and bishops of Ireland doing up his room in Maynooth in His Satanic Majesty's racing colours and sticking up pictures of all the horses his jockeys rode. The earl of Dublin, no less." This is an angry but accurate account of how the king was received at Ireland's preeminent Catholic seminary in July 1903. Bergan's and O'Molloy's jokes about "the women he rode" likewise have a foundation in historical fact. One of the crown prince's many scandalous sexual adventures took place nearby.

At more length

"Maynooth," founded in 1795, is an educational institution in the town of Maynooth, about fifteen miles west of Dublin in County Kildare. It has been known by various names: the Royal College of St Patrick, Maynooth; St Patrick's College, Maynooth; Maynooth College; Maynooth University; the Catholic University of Ireland, Maynooth; the National University of Ireland, Maynooth; St Patrick's Pontifical University. "Pontifical" means established or approved by the pope, and in the 19th century the college functioned chiefly as a seminary, educating and ordaining priests. Its Maynooth Cathechism was approved "for General Use throughout the Irish Church" in 1882. No other institution in Ireland more authoritatively represented Catholic faith.

Enter King Edward VII, a horse-racing aficionado who during his 1903 visit to Ireland was drawn to the horse country in County Kildare. On July 24 he and his wife Alexandra arrived in Maynooth by train and were cheered by crowds as they progressed from the station to the gates of the college. Twenty bishops and three archbishops greeted them there and showed them around, walking on red carpets laid down in the cloisters. Edward, who had been created "earl of Dublin" early in the reign of his mother when she visited Dublin, and who was aware of certain tensions between the two countries, emphasized his long ties to Ireland and recalled his previous trips there as Prince of Wales in 1861 and 1885. The former, when he underwent military training for ten weeks in County Kildare, had caused great scandal when some of his fellow officers smuggled an Irish actress named Nellie Clifden into his tent. This was not an isolated incident. When the Citizen says, "There's a bloody sight more pox than pax about that boyo," he is referring to Albert Edward's treatment for venereal disease acquired from one or more of his many mistresses.

Gifford summarizes the climactic event of the visit: "For the reception, the college refectory was decorated with his Brittanic majesty's racing colors and with engravings of two of his favorite horses, Diamond Jubilee and Ambush II. Monsignor Gerald Molloy (1834-1906), the rector of the university, gave an address of welcome. From an Irish point of view, the whole episode, including the unpriestly nature of the decorations, was an offensive demonstration of the Church's willingness to be subservient to the English Crown." Joe's contempt for these "holy boys" probably channels the feelings of the author, who was not only constitutionally anti-clerical but who saw an unholy alliance between the Roman church in Ireland and the English state in Ireland. His comment on "the horses his jockeys rode" prompts Alf to quip, "They ought to have stuck up all the women he rode himself." And J. J. O'Molloy, not to be outdone, remarks, "Considerations of space influenced their lordships' decision."

John Hunt 2026
